query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloys, the elevated temperature mechanical and thermal responses (stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic modulus) are primarily governed by thermally activated dislocation climb and dynamic recovery processes that are mediated by a uniform, refined microstructure. As the temperature increases from 500°C to 1200°C, these mechanisms lead to a pronounced drop in yield strength and elastic modulus and an increase in thermal expansion relative to the baseline state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or homogenized HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples characterized by controlled microstructural features (fixed grain size and phase uniformity).
generation.intervention: Conduct a series of high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., compression or tensile stress–strain measurements) and thermal expansion experiments on the alloy samples while keeping the microstructure constant. The tests should be performed in controlled increments over a temperature range from 500°C to 1200°C and under specified strain rates.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature regime from 500°C to 1200°C; mechanical tests under controlled strain rates (for example, between 0.001 s⁻¹ and 0.1 s⁻¹) and consistent heating profiles; and comparison with a baseline state established at lower temperatures (e.g., room temperature to 500°C).
generation.structural_mediator: The transition and activation of dislocation climb processes and dynamic recovery (or early-stage dynamic recrystallization) at high temperatures, which change the effective dislocation density and grain boundary mobility.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, increased thermal activation promotes dislocation climb, reducing obstacles for dislocation motion and leading to early yield and subsequent strain softening. Simultaneously, controlled microstructural conditions allow dynamic recovery (or dynamic reorganization of grain boundaries) to occur, which further influences the elastic modulus and thermal expansion behavior. These processes together cause the alloy's mechanical properties to deviate from those observed at lower temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline state (lower temperatures with minimal dislocation climb and recovery), the alloy will exhibit: 1) a significant decrease (e.g., >20% reduction) in yield strength and elastic modulus as temperature increases from 500°C to 1200°C; 2) an increase in the thermal expansion coefficient; and 3) a transition in the stress–strain curves from pronounced work hardening to earlier strain softening, indicative of the activated recovery mechanism.
generation.baseline: The mechanical and thermal responses (stress–strain curves and expansion behavior) measured at lower temperatures (room temperature up to 500°C) under identical microstructural conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within the temperature window of 500°C to 1200°C. Below 500°C, thermal activation is insufficient to trigger significant dislocation climb, and above 1200°C additional phase instabilities or competing mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative changes in yield strength, elastic modulus, and thermal expansion coefficients are not predetermined due to limited preliminary data in this temperature regime. Moreover, the extent of dynamic recovery versus dynamic recrystallization and their individual contributions remain to be clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of as-cast/homogenized HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled grain size. Subject these samples to high-temperature mechanical tests (stress–strain measurements) and thermal expansion studies at incremental temperatures (e.g., 500°C, 700°C, 900°C, and 1200°C) under a constant and defined strain rate. Concurrently, perform microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or SEM) to assess dislocation structures and evidence of dynamic recovery or recrystallization.
measurements: Yield strength, elastic modulus, and maximum stress from stress–strain curves
Microstructural analyses (grain size, evidence of dislocation climb/dynamic recovery, recrystallization features)
Dislocation density or defect state quantification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data does not show a significant (e.g., >20%) reduction in yield strength and elastic modulus or an increase in the thermal expansion coefficient with increasing temperature, or if microstructural analyses fail to reveal evidence of thermally activated dislocation climb/dynamic recovery mechanisms within 500°C to 1200°C, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

In this study, the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA were tested at elevated temperatures. Additionally, XRD, SEM, and TEM were used to thoroughly characterize the samples both before and after testing. The results are summarized below: Over a wide temperature range of RT-1223 K, the studied alloy exhibited excellent tensile mechanical properties. From RT to 678 K, the strength of the alloy was maintained above 1000 MPa; At 878–1078 K, the strength variation was small and no less than 800 MPa, and it nearly exceeded most commercial alloys. Coupled with an excellent cold workability, the alloy has the potential to be used as a new generation of high-temperature materials for the preparation of high-temperature-resistant parts in aerospace. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions showed similar trends at temperatures between 873 K and 1073 K. That is, a work hardening occurred after yielding, and then a gradual softening until fracture. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Here, the nano-indentation creep behavior was evaluated for two novel refractory high entropy alloys, HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr, at high load and elevated temperature. We performed two sets of experiments in the current study: (i) static constant load hold (CLH) protocol was adopted for one set of experiments to exclude possible surface effects and (ii) dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) mode was used to study oscillatory load and indentation size effect. This allowed the comparison of response from static and dynamic loads, for which there is no systematic study in literature. The effect of temperature on the creep behavior of the R-HEAs was also investigated systematically. Stress exponent, activation volume, and activation energy of alloys at different combinations of temperature and loads were compared with pure tungsten (W), a reference metal used in nuclear reactors [].
